{"self_assessment": "Impact: I built the bottom curve of the fish, the full lower half of the body, running from the nose to the tail join. It was connected all the way from the start domino, and it carries about half of the body outline the judge sees. The whole fish lit up from the nose when we traced it, about 99 of 101 standing dominoes. That gave the table a solid base to attach the tail to.

Execution: I laid the bottom curve in steady stretches by tracing the pad stroke, and it stayed connected from the nose. I then used close inspections of the join area at several points to check what the start would actually knock over. I did this at the tail join and again late in the build. These checks gave the table an accurate picture of what was connected. Once the fish was complete, I kept my hands off it to avoid bumping the run before the push.

Collaboration: Early on I made clear that I already had the bottom curve, so the others could move to the tail and the top curve instead of duplicating work. I offered to take over part of the top curve if it fell behind. I kept my hands out of the way while teammates worked on the joins, so nobody bumped each other. I gave clear updates on what looked connected from my side.

Leadership: I helped set the division of labor in the first minutes by claiming a stroke and pointing others to the open work. I kept the table coordinated around the shared goal of one connected fish. I pushed for a hands-off finish once the picture was complete, to protect the result. I think my part was a large share of the body outline, though I know the top curve and the tail were essential too.", "my_share_percent": 30}
